source_title: Patrick Stewart, ‘Star Trek’s’ Captain Picard and ‘X-Men’s’ Charles Xavier, Dies at 86

Patrick Stewart , the English actor with impressive stage and film credits who will be remembered most for his roles as Captain Jean-Luc Picard on “ Star Trek: The Next Generation ” and as Professor Charles Xavier in the “ X-Men ” films, died Wednesday at his Los Angeles home. He was 86.
According to a statement on his Instagram account, Stewart died after a brief battle with Alzheimer’s and Lewy Body Dementia. “His sonorous voice and singular talent will forever be synonymous with indelible performances in every genre. He explored the human condition in all its poetic complexity and brought hope not only to the far reaches of the Marvel Cinematic Universe, but into science fiction’s most iconic final frontier aboard the Starship Enterprise,” the statement read. “His professional accomplishments were humbly matched by his philanthropy and activism on behalf of human rights, survivors of domestic violence, global refugees, veterans’ mental health services, and animal welfare, particularly his cherished foster pitties. He was a Knight, Chancellor, motor sport enthusiast, and lifelong Huddersfield Football fan. He will be remembered for the dignity, compassion and humanity he brought to every role — in his art and life.”
Stewart and his “Star Trek: TNG” co-stars took their characters to the big screen for several films before the “Star Trek” film franchise was rebooted by J.J. Abrams with characters from the original series. He returned to the franchise for “Star Trek: Picard,” which ran from 2020 to 2023.
In the high-profile “X-Men” film franchise, Stewart played Professor Xavier opposite his good friend Ian McKellen as the villainous Magneto. He reprises the role in this December’s “Avengers: Doomsday” alongside McKellen.
In a 2008 profile describing Stewart’s return to his roots in classical theater by starring in a production of “Macbeth,” the New York Times in its mash-up headline pithily referenced the two very different paths the actor had followed in his career: “To Boldly Go Where Shakespeare Calls.”
In addition to being nominated for four Emmy awards, Stewart won three Olivier awards for his theater work and was nominated for a Tony Award.
It is hard to emphasize enough how dramatically Stewart’s life changed when he began his run on “Star Trek: The Next Generation” in 1987. For the two decades prior he had been a mainstay of the Royal Shakespeare Company. He had made time for some film and television work, but was kept busy appearing in more than two dozen RSC stage productions, including as Astrov in “Uncle Vanya” in 1974, Oberon in “A Midsummer Night’s Dream” in 1977, Shylock in “The Merchant of Venice” in 1978, and in the title role in “Titus Andronicus” in 1981.
Stewart played Picard throughout the 1987-1994 run of “Star Trek: TNG,” and then in the features “Star Trek: Generations” (in which he appeared with William Shatner), “Star Trek: First Contact,” “Star Trek: Insurrection” and “Star Trek: Nemesis.” He played Professor Xavier in “X-Men” (2000), “X-Men 2,” “X-Men: The Last Stand,” “X-Men Origins: Wolverine,” “The Wolverine” and “X-Men: Days of Future Past.”
Assessing Stewart’s contributions to “Star Trek: TNG,” the New York Times said, “With his aura of stern yet fair authority and seriousness of purpose, Mr. Stewart made Capt. Jean-Luc Picard the moral center of ‘Star Trek: The Next Generation’ across seven seasons, helping to keep it from sliding into camp or self-parody. Hollywood took to him, and he took to Hollywood.”
In general, Stewart seemed to keep a good sense of humor about his ties to popular culture, never publicly displaying the angst that Shatner and Leonard Nimoy each revealed at times. He did voicework on “The Simpsons,” “Family Guy” and “American Dad” and showed a willingness to make forays into comedy, playing a comically snooty waiter in Steve Martin’s 1991 gem “L.A. Story” and King Richard in Mel Brooks’ 1993 “Robin Hood: Men in Tights,” and hosting “Saturday Night Live” in 1994.
He recently voiced Sir Ritchfield in the animated “Sheep Detectives.”
In a very different vein, he was the best thing in 1995 gay comedy “Jeffrey”; the New York Times said Stewart “has some of the best lines and delivers them with a dignified brio that is only enhanced when he happens to be wearing a fuchsia beret, the uniform of an anti-gay-bashing group called the Pink Panthers.” Later the actor would serve as the narrator for Seth McFarlane’s scabrous comedy “Ted” and its sequel.
Stewart appeared in the 2015 film “Match,” based on the play by Stephen Belber, in which the actor played a vain, flamboyant dance instructor and — in a very different vein — in the Jeremy Saulnier horror-thriller “Green Room,” in which he played the leader of a band of neo-Nazis. He also starred in the Starz series “Blunt Talk,” about a substance-abusing English newscaster who moves to L.A. to host a talkshow.
Stewart continued his stage work even during the run of “Star Trek: TNG,” playing George in “Who’s Afraid of Virginia Woolf?” at the Young Vic in 1987 (he would return to the role at Minneapolis’ Guthrie Theatre in 2001) and repeatedly appearing in seasonal stagings in Los Angeles and on Broadway of a one-man version of “A Christmas Carol” that he adapted himself from the original Dickens.
After “TNG” ended, Stewart ramped up his theater work. He appeared on Broadway as Prospero in “The Tempest” in 1996, essayed the title role in a “photo-negative” staging of “Othello” at the Shakespeare Theatre in Washington, D.C., in 1997 and returned to Broadway to star in “The Ride Down Mt. Morgan” in 2000. In Britain, his work on the boards, starring in “Antony and Cleopatra,” in “The Tempest” and soon triumphing in “Macbeth,” won back the critics who had written him off when he had ventured into American television’s version of outer space years earlier. Also in 2008, Stewart played Claudius in a production of “Hamlet” that starred David Tennant, winning Stewart the Olivier award for best supporting actor.
Stewart had had a productive association with McKellen. In addition to starring as adversaries in the “X-Men” films, during the filming of which they developed a close friendship, the pair appeared on the West End in “Waiting for Godot” in 2009 and in repertory on Broadway in 2014 in that Beckett play and another existential classic, Harold Pinter’s “No Man’s Land.”
The actor made his first cinematic forays into fantasy and science fiction with John Boorman’s take on the Arthur legend, 1981’s “Excalibur,” in which Stewart played Leondegrance, and director David Lynch’s 1984 adaptation of Frank Herbert’s “Dune,” in which he played Gurney Halleck, a top officer in the Atreides household who becomes the trusted lieutenant to Paul (Kyle MacLachlan).
Earlier, on British television, he starred in the 1975 BBC miniseries “North & South,” an adaptation of the Elizabeth Gaskell novel, and then played Sejanus on “I, Claudius.” In the BBC’s “Maybury” from 1981-83 he starred as a psychiatrist at a hospital.
Patrick Hewes Stewart was born in Mirfield, Yorkshire, acting as a youth with various amateur drama societies in the region and leaving school at 15. He held a job as a newspaper reporter but ultimately chose acting over journalism. He lost his hair at age 18.
Stewart began his acting career at Manchester’s Library Theatre, after which he became a member of the Royal Shakespeare Company in 1966.
The actor lent his voice to a number of videogames associated with the “Star Trek” and “X-Men” franchises.
He was thrice married, the first time to choreographer Sheila Falconer, the second to Wendy Neuss, a producer of “Star Trek: The Next Generation.”
Survivors include third wife Sunny Ozell, whom he married in a 2013 ceremony presided over by Ian McKellen, as well as a daughter, Sophie Stewart, and son, actor Daniel Stewart, both from his marriage to Falconer.
Donations may be made to Johns Hopkins Alzheimer’s Disease Research Center Fund and Alzheimer’s Foundation of America Caregiver Resources .
